The geography of global compute is being redrawn by capital allocation decisions happening right now.

Google committed $15B to AI infrastructure in Finland, announced September 10, 2026. This is not a data center expansion. It is a strategic positioning decision — placing compute capacity near abundant clean energy, favorable regulatory environments, and subsea cable connectivity to multiple continents.

The same week, Qualcomm secured an AI chip deal with Amazon, signaling that hyperscalers are actively diversifying their silicon supply chains beyond Nvidia. Nvidia, still the dominant force at $5.1 trillion market cap, designs the GPUs that power most frontier models — but the supply chain is fragmenting by design.

For CEOs: these infrastructure commitments have a 3-5 year deployment horizon. The organizations that align their AI compute strategy with the emerging geography of capacity — not just today's availability — will secure cost and latency advantages that compound over time.

For CTOs: the Qualcomm-Amazon deal matters because it expands the inference hardware market. Multi-vendor silicon strategies will reduce concentration risk and create pricing leverage that did not exist 18 months ago.

The AI race is no longer just about models. It is about where compute lives, who controls the silicon, and which organizations locked in capacity before demand outstripped supply.
